title: Juniper and the Regiment
premise: In 1913, Ines Sandoval drives for suffragist leader Adela Marchetti, reading letters en route and believing invisibility is her safest armor. When a sealed letter reveals the Marchetti family has been named in a government plot to discredit the movement, Ines must carry the evidence through three military checkpoints to a journalist who can expose it. Betrayed by the one ally she trusted, she chooses loyalty to truth over belonging, delivering the letter at the cost of her position—and discovering that being seen was the freedom she'd been hiding from all along.
about_author: Mirabel Villalobos is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffragist correspondence in regional collections across the American Southwest. She writes historical fiction about the women history filed under 'assistant.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Ines Sandoval's POV. Establishes her routine: driving Adela Marchetti between suffrage meetings, sorting mail at red lights, memorizing what matters. She measures her life in portable things—a satchel, a spare tire, secrets. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Letters Before Their Time
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. We see her habit of reading letters before delivery—first as duty, then as addiction. A threatening note arrives for Adela; Ines pockets it, deciding what her employer needs to know. Beat: the first small betrayal, framed as protection.

chapters.title: The Marchetti Household
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Dinner at the Marchetti home introduces Adela's brother Tomás, a customs officer, and their fragile family politics. Ines watches from the edges, half-servant, half-confidante, belonging nowhere fully. Beat: longing sharpened by proximity.

chapters.title: Orders Come Down
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Rumors of a crackdown on the movement circulate; checkpoints appear on the roads north. Adela asks Ines to drive a route she's never driven. Beat: dread entering the ordinary, the world tightening.

chapters.title: What the Seal Concealed
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, the turn. Steam-softened by accident, a sealed letter opens: the Marchetti name appears in a forged document linking the family to an anarchist plot. Ines reads it twice as the engine idles. Beat: vertigo—the invisible woman holding everything.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She maps the route to journalist Rufina Ochoa in her head: the river bridge, the rail crossing, the garrison gate. Each will search her car. She rehearses lies while polishing the windshield. Beat: fear converted into method.

chapters.title: Tomás Asks Questions
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Tomás corners her at the house, probing whether Adela's mail has been 'irregular.' He suspects the leak came from inside. Ines lies fluently and hates how good she's become. Beat: guilt braided with resolve.

chapters.title: The Confession She Doesn't Make
chapters.summary: Adela's POV. Adela confides in Ines—not about the letter, but about her fears of surveillance, trusting her driver completely. Ines says nothing about what she knows. Beat: dramatic irony as intimacy becomes burden.

chapters.title: First Crossing: The River Bridge
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. With the evidence sewn into her coat lining, Ines crosses the bridge checkpoint. A young soldier searches the car but not her; her invisibility saves her. Beat: triumph shadowed by the realization that being unseen is a kind of erasure.

chapters.title: Rufina Ochoa's Back Room
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She reaches the newspaper office; Rufina verifies the forgery and promises publication—if Ines can bring the original signature page still held at the Marchetti house. Beat: hope, and a new, worse errand.

chapters.title: The Ally Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Fellow organizer Mateo, whom Ines has trusted for years, offers to help smuggle the second document. She hesitates, then agrees. Beat: warmth that the reader senses is wrong.

chapters.title: Second Crossing: The Rail Crossing
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The rail checkpoint has new orders: women traveling alone are detained. Ines talks her way through using Tomás's name, spending a piece of the family's trust like currency. Beat: the cost of each lie compounding.

chapters.title: Mateo's Price
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Mateo reveals he's been reporting to the authorities all along—he offers to let the story die if Ines hands over the letter and disappears. Beat: betrayal landing on the exact wound the book opened with: belonging bought with silence.

chapters.title: What Ines Carries
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, interior chapter. Hiding in a boardinghouse, she inventories her life again—satchel, coat, letter—and realizes the only thing she cannot carry is the self she built to survive. Beat: the thematic pivot toward choosing visibility.

chapters.title: Telling Adela
chapters.summary: Dual tension scene, mostly Ines's POV. Ines confesses everything: the read letters, the sealed document, Mateo. Adela's fury gives way to something harder—partnership. Beat: rupture becoming alliance; truth as the only real loyalty.

chapters.title: The Signature Page
chapters.summary: Ines and Adela's POV alternating. They retrieve the signature page from Tomás's locked desk during a household dinner, nearly caught when he returns early. Beat: high-wire suspense; the sisters-in-arms forged.

chapters.title: Third Crossing: The Garrison Gate
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The final checkpoint, where Mateo waits, having reported her. Ines is searched—but Adela arrives publicly, demanding her driver be released, making Ines visible to every soldier present. Beat: exposure as salvation.

chapters.title: Runaway Engine
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A chase sequence: Ines drives the mountain road with soldiers behind her, the documents against her heart, choosing speed over stealth for the first time. Beat: exhilaration replacing fear; identity claimed at full throttle.

chapters.title: Publication Morning
chapters.summary: Rufina's POV briefly, then Ines's. The exposé runs; the plot collapses under public scrutiny; Tomás resigns rather than face charges. Beat: vindication that tastes complicated—the family saved and wounded at once.

chapters.title: Reckonings
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Confrontations settle accounts: Mateo arrested, Adela offering Ines a real position, not a servant's role. Ines must decide whether to stay in a house where she was never quite home. Beat: bittersweet clarity.

chapters.title: The Letter She Writes Herself
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. For the first time, Ines writes a letter instead of reading one—to her estranged sister—sealing it herself and entrusting it to the mail unread by anyone, including her. Beat: release; trust extended outward at last.

chapters.title: Juniper and the Regiment
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, epilogue. Months later, Ines drives for the movement openly, her name printed in the article's byline thanks. Passing the river bridge, the young soldier salutes her—sees her—and she returns it. Beat: belonging earned through truth, not invisibility; the road open ahead.
